Continuum Attention

Afshin Khadangi Affiliation: SnT, University of Luxembourg Email: afshin.khadanki@uni.lu Affiliation: afshin.xyz
Abstract

We introduce Continuum Attention (CA), a causal Transformer attention operator that replaces discrete key and value lookup with integration over a continuous, piecewise linear memory curve. Each query induces an exponential relevance density along the curve. Integrating the density and interpolated values yields exact normalized attention from closed form exponential moments, including half token boundary contributions. The gradients follow analytically from moments of order at most two, enabling parallel GPU implementations while retaining quadratic sequence complexity and the standard Transformer decoder. Compared with ordinary softmax and focal attention, CA reduces mean validation negative log likelihood by 0.0200 and 0.0480 nats per byte, respectively, winning all paired comparisons. An additional disjoint validation slice yields a 0.0457 nats per byte advantage over the strongest selected softmax baseline, with a paired 95% confidence interval. These findings motivate continuous integration as a promising attention alternative while leaving larger scale generalization open.

1 Introduction

Attention mechanisms have become a fundamental component of modern neural networks, enabling representations to be constructed through content dependent interactions between queries, keys, and values Bahdanau et al. (2014); Vaswani et al. (2017). In the Transformer, scaled dot product attention assigns a normalized exponential weight to each available key and aggregates the corresponding value vectors. For a causal query at position ii, this operation takes the form

𝐨i=∑j=0iexp⁡(si​j)​𝐯j∑j=0iexp⁡(si​j),si​j=𝐪i⊤​𝐤jτ​dh,\mathbf{o}_{i}=\frac{\sum_{j=0}^{i}\exp(s_{ij})\mathbf{v}_{j}}{\sum_{j=0}^{i}\exp(s_{ij})},\qquad s_{ij}=\frac{\mathbf{q}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{k}_{j}}{\tau\sqrt{d_{h}}}, (1)

where τ>0\tau>0 controls the sharpness of the attention distribution and dhd_{h} denotes the attention head dimension.

This formulation represents memory through a finite collection of key and value vectors. Each memory position contributes through its individual relevance score, and normalization is performed over discrete positions. Although learned projections produce continuous vector representations, the aggregation operator evaluates these representations only at the sampled token positions. This distinction motivates an alternative representation in which adjacent memory vectors define a continuous trajectory and the query retrieves information through integration along that trajectory.

Previous research has explored alternative attention distributions Martins and Astudillo (2016), adaptive receptive fields, and computationally efficient attention operators Sukhbaatar et al. (2019); Choromanski et al. (2020); Dao et al. (2022). Continuous domain attention has also been studied through exponential families, sparse probability densities, and analytical differentiation Martins et al. (2020); Martins et al. (2022). A complementary mathematical perspective describes attention through integral operators acting on probability measures Vuckovic et al. (2021). These developments motivate further investigation of the relationship between the geometry of stored representations and the measure used to retrieve information from them.

Prior work established a general framework for continuous attention through probability densities over continuous domains, including continuous softmax and sparse distributions with analytical gradients Martins et al. (2020). Building on this foundation, Continuum Attention specifies a causal, content dependent construction directly from Transformer key and value representations. Adjacent memory vectors define piecewise linear trajectories, and each query induces an exponential relevance density whose segment integrals admit exact evaluation through exponential moments. This construction avoids fitting a separate continuous value function and supports direct integration into standard autoregressive Transformer layers.

We introduce Continuum Attention (CA), a causal attention operator that constructs a continuous memory trajectory from the key and value representations of a Transformer. Consecutive vectors are connected through piecewise linear interpolation, defining continuous functions 𝐤⁡(t)\mathbf{k}(t) and 𝐯⁡(t)\mathbf{v}(t) over memory position tt. Each query induces an exponential relevance density along this trajectory, and its output is obtained through normalized integration:

𝐨iCA=∫−1/2i+1/2exp(𝐪i⊤​𝐤​(t)τ​dh)𝐯(t)dt∫−1/2i+1/2exp(𝐪i⊤​𝐤​(t)τ​dh)dt.\boxed{\mathbf{o}_{i}^{\mathrm{CA}}=\frac{\displaystyle\int_{-1/2}^{i+1/2}\exp\left(\frac{\mathbf{q}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{k}(t)}{\tau\sqrt{d_{h}}}\right)\mathbf{v}(t)\,dt}{\displaystyle\int_{-1/2}^{i+1/2}\exp\left(\frac{\mathbf{q}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{k}(t)}{\tau\sqrt{d_{h}}}\right)\,dt}.} (2)

The integration domain includes constant extensions of the first and last visible memory vectors over half unit intervals. These boundary contributions preserve the intended token mass convention, including uniform weighting when all relevance scores are equal.

The defining property of CA is its query adaptive retrieval geometry. Within each Transformer layer and attention head, independently learned projections define a distinct memory trajectory. Each query determines a relevance density over that trajectory and thereby controls the effective retrieval locations within individual memory segments. Consequently, different queries can retrieve different interpolated values from the same stored key and value sequence. This adaptation emerges directly from the query dependent score function and remains present when the attention temperature is fixed.

The piecewise linear construction also provides an analytical advantage. Along each memory segment, the relevance score is an affine function of the interpolation coordinate. The exponential integrals therefore admit exact expressions in terms of moments

Jn​(Δ)=∫01un​exp⁡(Δ​u)​𝑑u,J_{n}(\Delta)=\int_{0}^{1}u^{n}\exp(\Delta u)\,du, (3)

where moments of orders zero and one determine the forward aggregation, and the second order moment completes the analytical score derivatives. The resulting operator can be evaluated using finite algebraic expressions, allowing implementation through parallel GPU operations. CA retains the quadratic sequence complexity of conventional dense attention and can be incorporated into a standard causal Transformer decoder.

We investigate CA through byte level language modeling on TinyStories Eldan and Li (2023). The experiments use a six layer Transformer with approximately five million parameters, five independent training seeds, and context lengths of 192 and 512 tokens. We compare CA against conventional softmax attention under matched model configurations, training budgets, and attention temperatures. With a fixed temperature of 0.300.30, CA reduces mean validation negative log likelihood by 0.02000.0200 and 0.04800.0480 nats per byte at the two context lengths, respectively, with improvements in all five paired seed comparisons at each length. On an additional disjoint evaluation slice, CA achieves an improvement of 0.04570.0457 nats per byte at 512 tokens over the development selected softmax baseline, with a paired 95% confidence interval of [0.0316,0.0598][0.0316,0.0598]. This additional evaluation is exploratory because the slice was previously examined during model comparisons. The results demonstrate promising small scale language modeling performance while motivating further evaluation at larger model sizes and on additional datasets.

The contributions of this work are an exact formulation of causal attention over interpolated memory trajectories, a query adaptive retrieval mechanism with analytical forward and backward expressions, parallel GPU implementations validated against numerical reference calculations, and controlled empirical comparisons with conventional softmax attention across multiple training seeds and context lengths.

2 Method

We formulate Continuum Attention (CA) as an exact integral operator over a continuous memory trajectory constructed from the key and value representations of a causal Transformer. The construction is applied independently within each attention head and Transformer layer. For clarity, we omit the layer and head indices throughout the derivation.

2.1 Continuous Memory Representation

Consider a sequence of TT token representations projected into queries, keys, and values:

𝐪i=WQ​𝐱i,𝐤i=WK​𝐱i,𝐯i=WV​𝐱i,\mathbf{q}_{i}=W_{Q}\mathbf{x}_{i},\qquad\mathbf{k}_{i}=W_{K}\mathbf{x}_{i},\qquad\mathbf{v}_{i}=W_{V}\mathbf{x}_{i}, (4)

where 𝐪i,𝐤i,𝐯i∈ℝdh\mathbf{q}_{i},\mathbf{k}_{i},\mathbf{v}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}} and dhd_{h} denotes the dimension of an attention head.

For a causal query at position ii, only memory positions j≤ij\leq i are accessible. We construct continuous key and value functions by interpolating adjacent memory vectors. For each interval [j−1,j][j-1,j], where 1≤j≤i1\leq j\leq i, let u=t−(j−1)∈[0,1]u=t-(j-1)\in[0,1] and define

𝐤j​(u)\displaystyle\mathbf{k}_{j}(u) =(1−u)​𝐤j−1+u​𝐤j,\displaystyle=(1-u)\mathbf{k}_{j-1}+u\mathbf{k}_{j}, (5)
𝐯j​(u)\displaystyle\mathbf{v}_{j}(u) =(1−u)​𝐯j−1+u​𝐯j.\displaystyle=(1-u)\mathbf{v}_{j-1}+u\mathbf{v}_{j}. (6)

These segments form continuous functions 𝐤⁡(t)\mathbf{k}(t) and 𝐯⁡(t)\mathbf{v}(t) over [0,i][0,i]. We extend both functions constantly over the intervals [−1/2,0][-1/2,0] and [i,i+1/2][i,i+1/2], using the first and last visible memory vectors, respectively.

The resulting memory representation preserves the original token ordering and causal visibility while providing well defined representations at every position along the memory trajectory.

2.2 Query Adaptive Relevance Density

Each query induces a relevance score over the continuous memory domain:

si​(t)=γdh​𝐪i⊤​𝐤​(t),s_{i}(t)=\frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{d_{h}}}\mathbf{q}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{k}(t), (7)

where γ>0\gamma>0 is the attention score gain. For a fixed attention temperature τ\tau, γ=1/τ\gamma=1/\tau.

Within segment jj, define the endpoint scores

ai​j=si​(j−1),bi​j=si​(j),Δi​j=bi​j−ai​j.a_{ij}=s_{i}(j-1),\qquad b_{ij}=s_{i}(j),\qquad\Delta_{ij}=b_{ij}-a_{ij}. (8)

Since the key trajectory is linear within the segment, the score is affine:

si​j​(u)=ai​j+u​Δi​j,u∈[0,1].s_{ij}(u)=a_{ij}+u\Delta_{ij},\qquad u\in[0,1]. (9)

The query therefore induces an exponential relevance density

pi(t)=exp⁡(si​(t))Zi,Zi=∫−1/2i+1/2exp(si(t))dt.p_{i}(t)=\frac{\exp(s_{i}(t))}{Z_{i}},\qquad Z_{i}=\int_{-1/2}^{i+1/2}\exp(s_{i}(t))\,dt. (10)

CA retrieves information by integrating the continuous value trajectory against this density:

𝐨i=∫−1/2i+1/2pi(t)𝐯(t)dt.\boxed{\mathbf{o}_{i}=\int_{-1/2}^{i+1/2}p_{i}(t)\mathbf{v}(t)\,dt}. (11)

The adaptation depends directly on the query and the geometry of neighboring keys. In particular,

Δi​j=γdh​𝐪i⊤​(𝐤j−𝐤j−1),\Delta_{ij}=\frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{d_{h}}}\mathbf{q}_{i}^{\top}(\mathbf{k}_{j}-\mathbf{k}_{j-1}), (12)

so different queries induce different relevance profiles over the same memory segments. Distinct learned projections across layers and heads further provide different memory trajectories and retrieval behavior.

2.3 Exact Segment Integration

The affine score in Eq. (9) allows the continuous integral to be evaluated exactly. Define the exponential moments

Jn​(Δ)=∫01un​exp⁡(Δ​u)​𝑑u,n∈{0,1,2}.J_{n}(\Delta)=\int_{0}^{1}u^{n}\exp(\Delta u)\,du,\qquad n\in\{0,1,2\}. (13)

For Δ≠0\Delta\neq 0, these moments admit the expressions

J0​(Δ)\displaystyle J_{0}(\Delta) =eΔ−1Δ,\displaystyle=\frac{e^{\Delta}-1}{\Delta}, (14)
J1​(Δ)\displaystyle J_{1}(\Delta) =(Δ−1)​eΔ+1Δ2,\displaystyle=\frac{(\Delta-1)e^{\Delta}+1}{\Delta^{2}}, (15)
J2​(Δ)\displaystyle J_{2}(\Delta) =(Δ2−2​Δ+2)​eΔ−2Δ3.\displaystyle=\frac{(\Delta^{2}-2\Delta+2)e^{\Delta}-2}{\Delta^{3}}. (16)

Their continuous limits at Δ=0\Delta=0 are J0​(0)=1J_{0}(0)=1, J1​(0)=1/2J_{1}(0)=1/2, and J2​(0)=1/3J_{2}(0)=1/3.

For a segment connecting positions j−1j-1 and jj, its unnormalized probability mass is

Mi​j\displaystyle M_{ij} =∫01exp⁡(ai​j+u​Δi​j)​𝑑u\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{1}\exp(a_{ij}+u\Delta_{ij})\,du
=eai​j​J0​(Δi​j).\displaystyle=e^{a_{ij}}J_{0}(\Delta_{ij}). (17)

Its contribution to the value numerator is

𝐔i​j\displaystyle\mathbf{U}_{ij} =∫01exp⁡(ai​j+u​Δi​j)​𝐯j​(u)​𝑑u\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{1}\exp(a_{ij}+u\Delta_{ij})\mathbf{v}_{j}(u)\,du
=eai​j[(J0(Δi​j)−J1(Δi​j))𝐯j−1\displaystyle=e^{a_{ij}}\Big[\big(J_{0}(\Delta_{ij})-J_{1}(\Delta_{ij})\big)\mathbf{v}_{j-1}
+J1(Δi​j)𝐯j].\displaystyle\hskip 105.27519pt+J_{1}(\Delta_{ij})\mathbf{v}_{j}\Big]. (18)

Thus, the contribution of each memory segment is obtained from the endpoint scores and values using a finite number of analytical operations.

Adaptive retrieval positions.

The normalized mean interpolation coordinate within segment jj is

μ⁡(Δi​j)=J1​(Δi​j)J0​(Δi​j).\mu(\Delta_{ij})=\frac{J_{1}(\Delta_{ij})}{J_{0}(\Delta_{ij})}. (19)

For Δ≠0\Delta\neq 0,

μ⁡(Δ)=11−e−Δ−1Δ,μ⁡(0)=12.\mu(\Delta)=\frac{1}{1-e^{-\Delta}}-\frac{1}{\Delta},\qquad\mu(0)=\frac{1}{2}. (20)

Consequently,

𝐔i​j=Mi​j​[(1−μ⁡(Δi​j))​𝐯j−1+μ⁡(Δi​j)​𝐯j].\mathbf{U}_{ij}=M_{ij}\Big[(1-\mu(\Delta_{ij}))\mathbf{v}_{j-1}+\mu(\Delta_{ij})\mathbf{v}_{j}\Big]. (21)

The function μ⁡(Δ)\mu(\Delta) increases monotonically from zero to one. Positive score differences shift the effective retrieval position toward the right endpoint, while negative differences shift it toward the left endpoint. Equal scores produce the midpoint of the segment.

This gives CA two complementary forms of query adaptation. The segment mass Mi​jM_{ij} determines how strongly a memory interval contributes, while μ⁡(Δi​j)\mu(\Delta_{ij}) determines where information is retrieved within that interval. Both quantities are determined analytically for each query.

2.4 Boundary Contributions and Normalization

To treat endpoint memory positions consistently, we include constant half unit extensions at both ends of the visible memory domain. Their contributions to the normalizer and value numerator are

Zicap\displaystyle Z_{i}^{\mathrm{cap}} =12​esi​(0)+12​esi​(i),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}e^{s_{i}(0)}+\frac{1}{2}e^{s_{i}(i)}, (22)
𝐔icap\displaystyle\mathbf{U}_{i}^{\mathrm{cap}} =12​esi​(0)​𝐯0+12​esi​(i)​𝐯i.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}e^{s_{i}(0)}\mathbf{v}_{0}+\frac{1}{2}e^{s_{i}(i)}\mathbf{v}_{i}. (23)

The complete normalization factor and numerator are

Zi\displaystyle Z_{i} =Zicap+∑j=1iMi​j,\displaystyle=Z_{i}^{\mathrm{cap}}+\sum_{j=1}^{i}M_{ij}, (24)
𝐔i\displaystyle\mathbf{U}_{i} =𝐔icap+∑j=1i𝐔i​j.\displaystyle=\mathbf{U}_{i}^{\mathrm{cap}}+\sum_{j=1}^{i}\mathbf{U}_{ij}. (25)

The final attention output is therefore

𝐨i=𝐔icap+∑j=1i𝐔i​jZicap+∑j=1iMi​j.\boxed{\mathbf{o}_{i}=\frac{\mathbf{U}_{i}^{\mathrm{cap}}+\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{i}\mathbf{U}_{ij}}{Z_{i}^{\mathrm{cap}}+\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{i}M_{ij}}.} (26)

For i=0i=0, the two half unit contributions together yield the output 𝐨0=𝐯0\mathbf{o}_{0}=\mathbf{v}_{0}.

The endpoint convention also ensures that when all visible key scores are equal, each discrete value receives identical total mass, and Eq. (26) reduces exactly to uniform causal attention.

Because the segment contributions are nonnegative, CA can equivalently be written as

𝐨i=∑j=0iwi​j​𝐯j,wi​j≥0,∑j=0iwi​j=1.\mathbf{o}_{i}=\sum_{j=0}^{i}w_{ij}\mathbf{v}_{j},\qquad w_{ij}\geq 0,\qquad\sum_{j=0}^{i}w_{ij}=1. (27)

The effective weights combine contributions from adjacent memory segments and the boundary terms. This representation allows CA to be integrated into a conventional Transformer attention block.

2.5 Analytical Differentiation

The forward operator admits exact analytical derivatives. The second order moment J2J_{2} is sufficient because both the key scores and values are linear within each memory segment.

Let ℒ\mathcal{L} denote the training objective, and let

𝐠i=∂ℒ∂𝐨i,ri​j=𝐠i⊤​(𝐯j−𝐨i).\mathbf{g}_{i}=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{o}_{i}},\qquad r_{ij}=\mathbf{g}_{i}^{\top}(\mathbf{v}_{j}-\mathbf{o}_{i}). (28)

For segment jj, the contribution to the gradient with respect to its left endpoint score is

∂ℒ∂si​(j−1)|seg​j\displaystyle\left.\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial s_{i}(j-1)}\right|_{\mathrm{seg}\,j} =eai​jZi[(J0−2J1+J2)ri,j−1\displaystyle=\frac{e^{a_{ij}}}{Z_{i}}\Big[\big(J_{0}-2J_{1}+J_{2}\big)r_{i,j-1}
+(J1−J2)ri​j],\displaystyle\hskip 51.21495pt+\big(J_{1}-J_{2}\big)r_{ij}\Big], (29)

where the moments are evaluated at Δi​j\Delta_{ij}.

The corresponding contribution to the right endpoint is

∂ℒ∂si​(j)|seg​j\displaystyle\left.\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial s_{i}(j)}\right|_{\mathrm{seg}\,j} =eai​jZi[(J1−J2)ri,j−1\displaystyle=\frac{e^{a_{ij}}}{Z_{i}}\Big[\big(J_{1}-J_{2}\big)r_{i,j-1}
+J2ri​j].\displaystyle\hskip 51.21495pt+J_{2}r_{ij}\Big]. (30)

Each endpoint receives the sum of the contributions from its incident segments. The first and last visible scores also receive the boundary contributions

∂ℒ∂si​(0)|cap\displaystyle\left.\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial s_{i}(0)}\right|_{\mathrm{cap}} =esi​(0)2​Zi​ri​0,\displaystyle=\frac{e^{s_{i}(0)}}{2Z_{i}}r_{i0}, (31)
∂ℒ∂si​(i)|cap\displaystyle\left.\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial s_{i}(i)}\right|_{\mathrm{cap}} =esi​(i)2​Zi​ri​i.\displaystyle=\frac{e^{s_{i}(i)}}{2Z_{i}}r_{ii}. (32)

The value gradients follow from the effective weights in Eq. (27):

∂ℒ∂𝐯j=∑i=jT−1wi​j​𝐠i.\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{v}_{j}}=\sum_{i=j}^{T-1}w_{ij}\mathbf{g}_{i}. (33)

Writing gi​jsg_{ij}^{s} for the complete derivative with respect to si​(j)s_{i}(j), the query and key gradients are

∂ℒ∂𝐪i\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{q}_{i}} =γdh​∑j=0igi​js​𝐤j,\displaystyle=\frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{d_{h}}}\sum_{j=0}^{i}g_{ij}^{s}\mathbf{k}_{j}, (34)
∂ℒ∂𝐤j\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{k}_{j}} =γdh​∑i=jT−1gi​js​𝐪i.\displaystyle=\frac{\gamma}{\sqrt{d_{h}}}\sum_{i=j}^{T-1}g_{ij}^{s}\mathbf{q}_{i}. (35)

For the learned gain variant, we parameterize γ=exp⁡(ρ)\gamma=\exp(\rho) independently for each layer and head. Its gradient is

∂ℒ∂ρ=∑i=0T−1∑j=0igi​js​si​(j).\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\rho}=\sum_{i=0}^{T-1}\sum_{j=0}^{i}g_{ij}^{s}s_{i}(j). (36)

These expressions provide analytical differentiation through the complete attention operator using exponential moments of order at most two.

2.6 Numerical Evaluation and Complexity

Direct evaluation of exponential moments can lose numerical precision when endpoint scores are nearly equal. We therefore evaluate the moment expressions using series expansions near Δ=0\Delta=0, with

Jn​(Δ)=∑r=0∞Δrr!​(n+r+1).J_{n}(\Delta)=\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}\frac{\Delta^{r}}{r!(n+r+1)}. (37)

For general score differences, we use numerically stable exponential expressions and scale the integrals relative to the larger endpoint score. The normalizer is computed after subtracting the maximum visible score for each query, preserving the normalized output. Efficient and numerically stable evaluation of exponential normalizers has also been investigated for conventional softmax attention Milakov and Gimelshein (2018).

All segment integrals can be evaluated independently. Their contributions are accumulated into the effective attention weights, followed by multiplication with the value matrix. This permits parallel GPU implementation without numerical quadrature or sequential integration over memory positions.

For a sequence of length TT and head dimension dhd_{h}, the attention computation requires 𝒪⁡(T2​dh)\mathcal{O}(T^{2}d_{h}) operations per head, matching the asymptotic complexity of dense softmax attention. An implementation that materializes the attention matrix requires 𝒪⁡(T2)\mathcal{O}(T^{2}) attention storage, while tiled implementations can accumulate segment contributions without retaining the entire matrix. The present experiments employ custom Metal kernels for the exact forward computation and analytical score gradients, validated against an independent numerical reference.

2.7 Integration into Causal Transformers

CA replaces the attention operator within each Transformer block while retaining the surrounding decoder architecture. Queries, keys, and values are obtained from the usual learned linear projections, and the head outputs are concatenated and projected back to the model dimension. Residual connections, normalization, feedforward layers, positional embeddings, and the language modeling objective are retained.

We investigate two primary gain configurations. The fixed gain variant, denoted CA-P, uses γ=1/0.30\gamma=1/0.30 in every attention head. The learned gain variant, denoted CA-H, initializes each head at the same gain and optimizes ρ\rho during training. Query adaptation through Eq. (12) occurs in both configurations.

The fixed gain formulation introduces no additional trainable parameters relative to a conventional softmax attention layer with the same projection dimensions. This enables a direct architectural comparison under matched model size, attention temperature, and training budget.

3 Experiments and Results

We evaluate Continuum Attention (CA) in autoregressive language modeling, focusing on predictive quality, attention temperature, training stability, and computational performance. Our experiments compare CA against conventional softmax attention under matched model architectures and training budgets. All reported quality results are obtained from five independent training seeds.

3.1 Experimental Setup

Dataset and evaluation task.

We conduct byte level language modeling on TinyStories Eldan and Li (2023). Each text is encoded as a sequence of UTF-8 bytes, giving a vocabulary of 256 symbols. The model predicts the next byte using the standard autoregressive cross entropy objective.

We construct the training corpus from the first 16 million bytes of the TinyStories training split. Development validation uses the first 2 million bytes of the official validation split. An additional evaluation corpus consists of a separate 4 million byte portion of the validation stream, disjoint from the development validation bytes.

Our primary metric is negative log likelihood (NLL), measured in nats per byte. We additionally report bits per byte (BPB), computed as

BPB=NLLln⁡2.\mathrm{BPB}=\frac{\mathrm{NLL}}{\ln 2}. (38)

Lower values indicate better predictive performance.

Model architecture.

All experiments use the same causal Transformer decoder architecture Vaswani et al. (2017). The network contains six Transformer blocks, model width 256, four attention heads, and head dimension 64. Each block uses RMS normalization Zhang and Sennrich (2019), residual connections, and a SwiGLU feedforward network with hidden dimension 720 Shazeer (2020).

The model employs learned absolute positional embeddings, a vocabulary embedding of dimension 256, and an output projection tied to the input embedding matrix. The attention operator is the principal architectural variable across experiments.

At context length 192, fixed temperature models contain 5,008,640 trainable parameters. At context length 512, they contain 5,090,560 parameters. The difference arises from the larger positional embedding table. Variants with learned attention gains introduce 24 additional scalar parameters, corresponding to four heads in each of six layers.

Attention configurations.

We compare eight configurations, divided into conventional softmax attention and CA variants.

The conventional softmax controls are:

  • •

    B0.20\mathrm{B}_{0.20}, B0.30\mathrm{B}_{0.30}, and B0.50\mathrm{B}_{0.50}: softmax attention with fixed temperatures τ∈{0.20,0.30,0.50}\tau\in\{0.20,0.30,0.50\}.

  • •

    F\mathrm{F}: softmax attention with a learned positive gain initialized at effective temperature τ=1\tau=1.

  • •

    G\mathrm{G}: softmax attention with a learned positive gain initialized at effective temperature τ=0.30\tau=0.30.

The CA configurations are:

  • •

    S\mathrm{S}: CA with learned attention gains initialized at effective temperature τ=1\tau=1.

  • •

    H\mathrm{H}: CA with learned attention gains initialized at effective temperature τ=0.30\tau=0.30.

  • •

    P\mathrm{P}: CA with fixed attention temperature τ=0.30\tau=0.30.

For learned gain variants, every attention head has a positive scale parameter γ=exp⁡(ρ)\gamma=\exp(\rho), giving effective temperature τ=exp⁡(−ρ)\tau=\exp(-\rho). The fixed configurations B0.30\mathrm{B}_{0.30} and P\mathrm{P} therefore have identical parameter counts, identical initial score scaling, and the same surrounding Transformer architecture. Similarly, G\mathrm{G} and H\mathrm{H} provide matched comparisons with learned attention gains.

Optimization protocol.

All models are trained with AdamW Loshchilov and Hutter (2017), using learning rate 4×10−44\times 10^{-4}, momentum coefficients (β1,β2)=(0.9,0.95)(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.95), weight decay 0.10.1, and gradient norm clipping at 1.01.0. The learning rate is held constant during training.

Learned attention gain parameters receive eight times the base learning rate and no weight decay. All other optimization settings remain identical across attention variants.

We use five training seeds:

{1729, 2718, 3141, 4567, 6174}.\{1729,\ 2718,\ 3141,\ 4567,\ 6174\}.

The two context configurations receive equal training token budgets:

T=192:\displaystyle T=192: 8×192×2500=3,840,000,\displaystyle 8\times 192\times 2500=3{,}840{,}000, (39)
T=512:\displaystyle T=512: 2×512×3750=3,840,000.\displaystyle 2\times 512\times 3750=3{,}840{,}000.

Here the factors correspond to batch size, sequence length, and optimization steps. Each variant uses the same training sample sequence for a given seed and context length. Models are evaluated at the final training step, with no checkpoint selection based on validation performance.

The study contains 80 completed training runs: eight attention configurations, five seeds, and two context lengths.

Validation protocol.

Development NLL is estimated using 128 sampled validation batches with evaluation seed 9090, shared across all configurations. The additional evaluation uses 256 sampled batches with evaluation seed 121212.

All comparisons use paired training seeds and identical evaluation sampling within each context. We report the mean NLL over five seeds and paired 95% Student tt confidence intervals for the NLL differences. For paired differences δ1,…,δ5\delta_{1},\ldots,\delta_{5}, the interval is

δ¯±t0.975,4​sδ5,\bar{\delta}\pm t_{0.975,4}\frac{s_{\delta}}{\sqrt{5}}, (40)

where sδs_{\delta} is the sample standard deviation of the paired differences.

These intervals characterize variation across the five training seeds on the fixed evaluation samples. They are reported without correction for multiple comparisons.

3.2 Development Validation Results

Table 1 reports mean validation NLL for all eight attention configurations at the two context lengths.

The results reveal an important dependence on attention temperature. The original CA configuration S\mathrm{S}, initialized at effective temperature 11, improves upon the correspondingly initialized softmax control F\mathrm{F}. However, fixed temperature softmax with τ=0.30\tau=0.30 achieves lower NLL than S\mathrm{S} at both context lengths. This motivates comparisons in which both operators receive identical attention scaling.

Under these matched conditions, CA achieves the lowest mean validation NLL at both context lengths. The fixed temperature variant P\mathrm{P} improves over B0.30\mathrm{B}_{0.30} by 0.0200160.020016 nats per byte at T=192T=192 and 0.0480450.048045 nats per byte at T=512T=512. These correspond to relative NLL reductions of approximately 1.94%1.94\% and 4.09%4.09\%, respectively.

The improvement is consistent across all five paired seeds at both context lengths. At T=192T=192, the paired 95% confidence interval for the improvement is [0.013779,0.026253][0.013779,0.026253]. At T=512T=512, the corresponding interval is [0.033504,0.062587][0.033504,0.062587].

The learned gain comparison produces a similar trend. CA variant H\mathrm{H} improves over softmax variant G\mathrm{G} by 0.0123890.012389 nats per byte at T=192T=192 and 0.0726980.072698 nats per byte at T=512T=512. The corresponding confidence intervals are [−0.004571,0.029349][-0.004571,0.029349] and [0.030012,0.115383][0.030012,0.115383]. Although H\mathrm{H} wins all five paired seeds at both lengths, the interval at T=192T=192 includes zero.

3.3 Fixed and Learned Attention Gains

We further examine whether the attention gain must be learned to obtain the benefits of continuous integration.

At T=192T=192, fixed temperature CA P\mathrm{P} outperforms learned gain CA H\mathrm{H} by 0.0038200.003820 nats per byte on average. The paired 95% confidence interval is [−0.003918,0.011558][-0.003918,0.011558].

At T=512T=512, the corresponding mean advantage of P\mathrm{P} is 0.0011490.001149 nats per byte, with confidence interval [−0.014050,0.016348][-0.014050,0.016348].

Neither comparison establishes a clear advantage for learning the gain. The fixed temperature configuration provides competitive or better mean performance in both contexts while preserving exact parameter equality with the fixed temperature softmax baseline.

These observations motivate the use of P\mathrm{P} as the primary CA configuration in the remaining analysis. Its query adaptation arises from the continuous relevance density and segment integration, independently of learned temperature parameters.

3.4 Evaluation on Disjoint Validation Text

We evaluate the saved model checkpoints on an additional 4 million byte portion of TinyStories validation text, disjoint from the development validation corpus.

During the original experiment, the strongest softmax control was selected using development validation: G\mathrm{G} for T=192T=192 and B0.30\mathrm{B}_{0.30} for T=512T=512. These selections were frozen before the original evaluation of S\mathrm{S}.

Subsequently, the H\mathrm{H} and P\mathrm{P} ablations were introduced and evaluated on the same previously examined validation portion. We therefore treat their results as exploratory measurements. The evaluation samples and original softmax results are reused without retraining the controls.

Table 2 reports the mean NLL over five seeds.

Both temperature adjusted CA variants achieve lower mean NLL than the development selected softmax baseline at both context lengths.

For the primary fixed temperature CA variant, the mean improvement is 0.0163680.016368 nats per byte at T=192T=192, with paired 95% confidence interval [−0.000134,0.032870][-0.000134,0.032870]. All five paired seeds favor CA, although the confidence interval includes zero.

At T=512T=512, fixed temperature CA improves mean NLL by 0.0457410.045741 nats per byte relative to B0.30\mathrm{B}_{0.30}, with confidence interval [0.031634,0.059848][0.031634,0.059848]. The improvement occurs in all five paired seeds.

Learned gain CA H\mathrm{H} similarly achieves an improvement of 0.0469900.046990 nats per byte at T=512T=512, with confidence interval [0.024375,0.069606][0.024375,0.069606] and five wins across five seeds.

The results support a consistent performance advantage for temperature adjusted CA at context length 512 in this experimental setting. At context length 192, the exploratory results favor CA in mean NLL, with greater uncertainty across training seeds.

Table 3 summarizes the principal paired comparisons.

3.5 Computational Performance

We measure computational performance on Apple Silicon using PyTorch 2.8 and the Metal Performance Shaders backend. Conventional softmax attention uses the PyTorch scaled dot product attention interface. CA uses custom Metal implementations of the exact segment integration and analytical score gradients.

At context length 192, the CA implementation uses the metal_analytic backend. At context length 512, it uses the metal_long backend.

Training throughput includes the model forward pass, backward pass, and optimization steps. Forward throughput is measured separately over repeated full sequence inference calls.

Table 4 reports mean throughput across the five training seeds.

At context length 192, fixed temperature CA achieves training throughput comparable to conventional softmax. At context length 512, CA P\mathrm{P} is approximately 7.3%7.3\% slower in training throughput and 39.1%39.1\% slower in forward throughput than the matched softmax control.

The larger forward performance gap reflects the current implementation and provides an important optimization target. These measurements characterize the tested Metal kernels and context lengths.

Numerical verification.

Before CA training, the Metal kernels are checked against an independent CPU reference using double precision calculations. The recorded maximum absolute deviation for the analytical score gradients across the experiment preflight checks is below 6×10−76\times 10^{-7}. All preflight checks pass at both context lengths.

4 Discussion and Limitations

Continuous memory retrieval.

Continuum Attention extends the conventional attention operator by defining a continuous memory trajectory through adjacent key and value representations. Its principal distinction lies in the integration of query dependent relevance over this trajectory. Each memory segment contributes both an analytical probability mass and an effective retrieval position, determined by the exponential moments of its endpoint score difference.

This construction introduces a structured relationship between neighboring memory positions. While conventional softmax attention assigns relevance to individual sampled keys, CA integrates relevance across the intervals connecting them. The resulting retrieval positions adapt to each query, with independently learned projections providing distinct memory trajectories across Transformer layers and heads. This adaptation remains present under a fixed attention temperature.

The continuous formulation also admits an equivalent discrete representation with nonnegative attention weights that sum to one. Consequently, CA preserves the normalized aggregation structure of conventional attention while modifying how the effective weights are determined. Its output remains a convex combination of the original value vectors.

Attention temperature and architectural effects.

The temperature ablations reveal the importance of controlling attention score scaling when evaluating alternative attention mechanisms. CA with learned gains initialized at effective temperature 11 outperforms the corresponding softmax configuration, but stronger softmax controls achieve better validation performance after temperature adjustment.

When both operators use a fixed temperature of 0.300.30, CA achieves lower mean validation NLL across all five paired seeds at context lengths 192 and 512. The corresponding improvements are 0.02000.0200 and 0.04800.0480 nats per byte, respectively. Both paired 95% confidence intervals exclude zero.

The fixed temperature CA variant also performs comparably to the variant with learned attention gains. This observation suggests that the benefits measured in our experiments arise from the continuous integration operator under suitable score scaling, without requiring additional learned temperature parameters. The fixed configuration therefore provides a particularly direct comparison with softmax attention, preserving both parameter count and attention temperature.

Relation to continuous attention.

Continuous attention distributions and analytical differentiation have previously been investigated Martins et al. (2020); Martins et al. (2022). CA builds on this mathematical foundation through a specific construction for causal Transformer memory. It uses the Transformer keys themselves to define a piecewise linear score trajectory and interpolates the corresponding values directly, allowing each segment integral to be evaluated exactly.

The contribution is therefore centered on the particular memory representation, its exact exponential moment formulation, and its implementation within autoregressive Transformer layers. Further comparisons with alternative continuous attention parameterizations would help isolate the influence of this particular interpolation geometry.

Computational considerations.

CA retains the quadratic sequence complexity of dense attention. Exact segment integration introduces additional arithmetic relative to ordinary softmax, including exponential moment evaluation and the redistribution of probability mass between neighboring values.

Our Metal implementation achieves training throughput comparable to softmax at context length 192. At context length 512, the fixed temperature CA variant exhibits approximately 7.3%7.3\% lower training throughput and 39.1%39.1\% lower forward throughput. These results indicate a computational tradeoff between the observed modeling improvements and the additional cost of continuous integration. More efficient kernel designs, particularly those that reduce intermediate memory traffic, remain an important direction for implementation research.

Limitations.

Our empirical investigation is restricted to approximately five million parameter Transformers trained on a byte level subset of TinyStories. The experiments use two context lengths, a common training budget of 3.84 million tokens per model, and five independent training seeds. Evaluation on larger models, additional language modeling corpora, and longer contexts is needed to assess the generality of the observed improvements. Our experiments use learned absolute positional embeddings. Evaluating CA with alternative positional representations, including rotary position embeddings Su et al. (2024), remains an open direction.

The additional disjoint validation slice was examined during earlier model comparisons before the final CA temperature ablations were introduced. Its results therefore provide exploratory evidence. Although the 512 token comparison yields a positive paired confidence interval across all five seeds, the reported intervals reflect training seed variation on fixed evaluation samples and include no correction for multiple model comparisons. A new, previously unexamined evaluation corpus would provide stronger confirmatory evidence.

The current experiments also examine a limited selection of CA temperature configurations. More extensive optimization of both CA and conventional softmax may alter their relative performance. Furthermore, the continuous trajectories are constructed through linear interpolation between adjacent learned representations. The usefulness of this geometric assumption may depend on the data, learned representations, and context length. Interpolated locations need not correspond to independently meaningful memory states.

Finally, the present experiments establish predictive improvements under controlled small model conditions. They do not yet establish corresponding gains in larger language models, broader downstream tasks, or overall computational efficiency. These questions motivate further empirical and theoretical investigation.

5 Conclusion

We introduced Continuum Attention, a causal attention operator that performs exact integration over continuous memory trajectories constructed from Transformer keys and values. Piecewise linear interpolation enables closed form evaluation through exponential moments, while query dependent relevance determines both the probability mass and effective retrieval position within each memory segment. Analytical gradients and parallel GPU implementations allow the method to operate within conventional Transformer decoders while preserving quadratic sequence complexity.

In controlled byte level language modeling experiments, CA with fixed attention temperature outperformed matched softmax attention across five training seeds at context lengths 192 and 512. The results demonstrate promising predictive benefits from continuous memory integration without additional trainable parameters. Further work will investigate larger model scales, broader datasets, longer contexts, and more efficient implementations to determine the practical scope of these findings.
